newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Team of doctors await return of Mir commander.
newsitem.headline: Team of doctors await return of Mir commander.

text.p: Extra doctors were awaiting the returning commander of Russia's Mir space station on Thursday to check on a cardiac problem he developed during six tense months in orbit.
If his heart is up to it, a bottle of his favourite French red wine awaits 43-year-old Vasily Tsibliyev when he lands.

"We have strengthened the team and taken on additional specialists -- a cardiologist from the military hospital and an intensive care doctor as well as additional medication," said deputy flight director Igor Goncharov, who is also chief doctor.
"There could be unforseen situations, so we have taken these measures," he told Reuters in Dzhezkazgan, the nearest town to the landing site in the ex-Soviet republic of Kazakhstan.
The descent from Mir to the Kazakh steppe where their Soyuz craft is due to touch down at 1616 Moscow time (1216 GMT) on Thursday will take the cosmonauts less than four hours.
They are wearing special light space suits introduced after a tragedy in 1971 when operators opened the hatch on a returning space capsule to find all three crew had died on the way down.
As they plunge to earth, commander Tsibliyev and engineer Alexander Lazutkin, 39, will undergo huge weight changes and are likely to lose control over their bodily functions.

Medical staff who will fly to the capsule in helicopters will transfer them to a tent to clean them up and make sure they are in good enough health to fly by helicopter to a plane which will take them to Moscow to be reunited with their families.
Tsibliyev, who developed an irregular heart beat after the worst accident in Mir's history slashed power supply to the 11-year-old station, is no longer taking medication.
Space officials said he felt responsible following the crash, which President Boris Yeltsin has said may have been caused by human error.
"In recent days he's been in a satisfactory condition and with no complaints. I talked to him yesterday and he was in good spirits," Goncharov said.
"He will be under special observation in the coming days and follow a rehabilitation programme set according to his health."

Tsibliyev's wife Larissa has sent him a bottle of his favourite French red wine. Alcohol is forbidden in space except for special occasions but the two men will be allowed to drink a little after landing.
Other gifts sent by the cosmonauts' families, who are waiting for them at Star City, include boiled potatoes, fresh cucumbers and tomatoes and salted pork fat -- a regional speciality.

Star City doctors flying with top space officials to Kazakhstan had picked out a big watermelon for the crew. They were also carrying cognac and vodka, though whether for the crew or themselves was not clear.
Vladimir Krivolapov, a doctor on the team, said Tsibliyev's wife would greet him at Star City with a huge bunch of flowers.
He said the pair were looking forward to taking a shower and a bath on Thursday evening after six months having to make do with sponging themselves.
The shower system on Mir had broken down -- just one of a series of glitches aboard the station, now limping along on half power after the crash with a supply ship on June 25.
